title: From Ash-Shu'ara to Ya-Sin
intro: 30 days through surahs 26 to 36, from Ash-Shu'ara to Ya-Sin, one verse at a time.

posts.display: Who created me, and He doth guide me, And Who feedeth me and watereth me. And when I sicken, then He healeth me.
posts.caption: This plan walks through surahs 26 to 36, beginning with Ash-Shu'ara, "The Poets", a Meccan surah of 227 verses, second only to Al-Baqarah in number of verses. Here the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) describes his Lord to his idol-worshipping people: the One who creates, guides, feeds and heals him.

The prayer of the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) turns to the Day of Judgment, when wealth and children are of no use. What counts is coming to Allah with a qalb salim, a sound or whole heart, which commentators variously describe as free of shirk, doubt and spite. It is a much-loved phrase among Muslims.

Near the end of the surah, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is told to put his trust (tawakkul) in Allah, who sees him standing in prayer and moving among those who bow down in worship. The pair of names al-Aziz ar-Rahim, the Mighty, the Merciful, closes each story in this surah as a refrain.

An-Naml, "The Ant", is a Meccan surah of 93 verses named after this scene. As the Prophet Sulayman (Solomon) and his armies approach, an ant warns the others to take cover, since the army would not even notice them. Sulayman, who the Quran says was taught the speech of birds, hears her and smiles.

posts.display: Lo! it is from Solomon, and lo! it is: In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful.
posts.caption: The Queen of Sheba reads out a letter from the Prophet Sulayman (Solomon), and it opens with the Bismillah. This is the only place the Bismillah appears in the middle of a surah. Since At-Tawbah has none at its start, the phrase still appears 114 times in the Quran, once for each surah.

One of a series of questions in An-Naml asking who truly provides and protects. This one, about the One who answers the desperate when they call, is a verse many Muslims turn to in hardship. "The wronged one" renders al-mudtarr, someone in dire need, and "viceroys" means successors.

Al-Qasas, "The Story", is a Meccan surah of 88 verses that tells the life of the Prophet Musa (Moses) in detail. It begins with his mother: Pharaoh is killing the sons of the Israelites, and she is inspired to set her baby on the river. The promise to return him to her is kept a few verses later.

The Prophet Musa (Moses) has fled Egypt and reaches Midian alone, with nothing. He waters the flocks of two women who had been holding back from the crowded well, then sits in the shade and says this short prayer. Help arrives in the very next verse, and many Muslims repeat the prayer when in need.

posts.display: But seek the abode of the Hereafter in that which Allah hath given thee and neglect not thy portion of the world, and be thou kind even as Allah hath been kind to thee.
posts.display_original: وَٱبْتَغِ فِيمَآ ءَاتَىٰكَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلدَّارَ ٱلْـَٔاخِرَةَ وَلَا تَنسَ نَصِيبَكَ مِنَ ٱلدُّنْيَا وَأَحْسِن كَمَآ أَحْسَنَ ٱللَّهُ إِلَيْكَ
posts.caption: Qarun (Korah), from the people of the Prophet Musa (Moses), grew arrogant with enormous wealth. These words are part of the advice his own people gave him, often quoted as a picture of balance between this life and the next. "Be thou kind" renders ahsin, from ihsan, doing good and doing it well.

Al-Qasas ends with a declaration of Allah's oneness and the passing of all things. "Countenance" renders wajh, literally "face". Classical commentators explain it as Allah Himself, or as whatever is done for His sake; only that remains.

Al-Ankabut, "The Spider", is a surah of 69 verses, usually classed as Meccan. It opens by asking whether people think that simply declaring faith will spare them from being tested. Many commentators link it to the early Muslims of Mecca, who faced persecution for their faith.

The surah takes its name from this parable. Relying on anything other than Allah for protection is compared to a spider's house, which looks like a shelter but is the flimsiest of all. "Patrons" renders awliya', protectors or allies.

According to classical commentators, some believers feared that leaving Mecca for a new home would leave them without a living. The verse answers with a picture: countless creatures cannot carry or store their own food, yet Allah provides for them as He provides for people. It is often recalled when speaking of tawakkul, trust in Allah.

Ar-Rum, "The Romans", is a Meccan surah of 60 verses, named for its opening lines about the war between the Byzantine Romans and Persia. This verse, one of a series of "signs", is often read at Muslim weddings: love (mawadda) and mercy (rahma) are gifts placed between spouses. "Helpmeets" means spouses.

Another of the signs in Ar-Rum: the variety of human languages and colours is presented as part of Allah's design, alongside the creation of the heavens and the earth. "Men of knowledge" renders al-alimin, those who know and reflect.

A whole life in one verse: weakness as a baby, strength in adulthood, then weakness and grey hair in old age. The Quran presents each stage as Allah's shaping. It sits near the end of Ar-Rum, among verses about Allah bringing life out of death.

Luqman is a Meccan surah of 34 verses named after Luqman, a sage the Arabs already knew for his wisdom; most scholars regard him as a wise man rather than a prophet. The Quran says he was given wisdom (hikma), and the first thing he is told is to be grateful. His advice to his son follows.

Luqman's advice to his son begins with not associating anything with Allah. Here he teaches how complete Allah's knowledge is: even a deed the weight of a mustard seed, hidden in a rock or anywhere in creation, will be brought to light. "Subtile" renders al-Latif, the Subtle and Gentle.

Luqman's next advice turns from belief to action: keep up the prayer, encourage what is right, discourage what is wrong, and bear patiently whatever comes. "Persevere" renders isbir, from sabr, and "the steadfast heart of things" means matters that call for firm resolve.

Luqman ends his advice with manners: not turning one's face from people in contempt, not strutting, keeping a modest stride and a lowered voice. The blunt image of a donkey's bray makes the point memorable. "Turn not thy cheek" means turning one's face away in arrogance.

As-Sajdah, "The Prostration", is a Meccan surah of 30 verses, named for the prostration described in verse 15. These verses describe people who leave their beds to pray in fear and hope, and promise them a joy kept hidden, beyond what anyone knows. Many Muslims connect this with tahajjud, voluntary night prayer.

Al-Ahzab, "The Confederates", is a Medinan surah of 73 verses, named after the allied tribes that besieged Medina around 627 CE. Amid that hardship, this verse holds up the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ as an excellent example (uswa hasana) for anyone who hopes in Allah and the Last Day.

This verse is the basis of the salawat, the blessings Muslims say whenever the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is mentioned. Sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, "Allah bless him and grant him peace", is what the symbol after his name stands for. Muslims also send blessings on him in the daily prayers.

posts.display: Give thanks, O House of David! Few of My bondmen are thankful.
posts.display_original: ٱعْمَلُوٓا۟ ءَالَ دَاوُۥدَ شُكْرًا وَقَلِيلٌ مِّنْ عِبَادِىَ ٱلشَّكُورُ
posts.caption: Saba, "Sheba", is a Meccan surah of 54 verses named after the ancient kingdom in southern Arabia. Here the family of the Prophet Dawud (David) is told to give thanks. The Arabic literally says "work, in gratitude", which commentators take to mean thanks shown in deeds, not only in words.

The people of Sheba lived between two great gardens, in a good land under a forgiving Lord. The next verses tell how they turned away and the gardens were lost to a flood. Many commentators and historians connect it with the ancient dam at Marib in Yemen. "Indulgent" renders ghafur, forgiving.

Fatir, "The Originator", is a Meccan surah of 45 verses, also called Al-Mala'ikah, "The Angels". Like Saba before it, it opens with praise of Allah. This second verse is a well-loved reassurance: no one can hold back the mercy Allah opens, and no one can release what He withholds.

Humanity is addressed directly: people are the poor, the ones in need (fuqara'), before Allah, while He alone is free of all need. "The Absolute" is Pickthall's word for al-Ghani, the Self-Sufficient, and "Owner of Praise" renders al-Hamid, the Praiseworthy.

Ya-Sin, a Meccan surah of 83 verses, is popularly called "the heart of the Quran" and is often recited for the sick, the dying and the dead. This verse says Allah records not only what people do but their footprints, which commentators explain as their steps and the traces they leave behind.

Ya-Sin pictures the people of Paradise resting in the shade with all that they ask for. Then comes this greeting, salamun qawlan min rabbin rahim, a word of peace from a merciful Lord. Commentators note that this greeting of peace comes directly from Allah Himself.

Ya-Sin ends with Allah's creative command, kun fa-yakun, and the glorification of the One who holds dominion over all things. "Dominion" renders malakut, sovereignty over the whole of creation. That closes this journey from Ash-Shu'ara to Ya-Sin; thank you for reading along.
